brief.head: No cricket next time
brief.text: Reboot civilisation from human nature alone, Amit Varma said, and money and football would probably return. Cricket would not: “It’s a historical accident.” {063-C04}

brief.head: Prison mathematics
brief.text: Thrown into solitary confinement with only pen and paper, Ajay Shah would rebuild all the mathematics he knows. “Now rebuild the whole damn edifice from scratch,” he said. {063-S03}

brief.head: Chess needs company
brief.text: Stefan Zweig’s prisoner mastered chess against himself. Amit Varma argued a human brain hits a ceiling that way: every game with an opponent is a conversation. {063-C11}

brief.head: Beat the sugar pill
brief.text: In one wartime story, a patient told he had been given anaesthetic felt nothing during surgery. So a medicine must beat a placebo, Amit Varma said, not merely nothing. {063-C10}

brief.head: Why quackery caught on
brief.text: Homeopathy spread in the 19th century, Amit Varma said, when bloodletting was the cure for most things. Sugar pills at least would not kill you. {063-S10}

thought.text: But if you’re not actively doing something, it will go away.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what humanity forgets
lead.head: What the ocean of time took
body: Ajay Shah opened with a warning. We think of knowledge as wealth that only grows, he said, but “in this episode today, we’re going to scare the bejesus out of you on this.”

Amit Varma began with a witch. In a thought experiment by the writer Tim Urban, a wicked witch makes every material good on Earth vanish. That leaves 7.3 billion naked people with all their knowledge in their heads, and a note: build one working iPhone 6S and everything comes back. {063-S01}
How long would that take? “Never,” said Shah. “It’s impossible.”

Without markets, laws and institutions, he said, “there is no way to feed seven and a half billion people.” Humanity would sink into barbarism, and the population would crash to 10 million. A new civilisation would rise, but never by the same path to touch screens.
## Sediment and the sea

Varma framed the theme with a line from a poem by Philip Larkin, in which misery “deepens like a coastal shelf”. We like to think knowledge builds that way, each generation laying down a layer and standing on the shoulders of giants.
“So maybe it’s a good metaphor,” he said, “because a lot of the sedimentary layers get washed away by the ocean of time.” {063-C01}
Some lost knowledge has been regained, some is still being chased and some may never come back. The hosts told five such quests.
## Five quests
Silphium, a herb the Romans called the food of the gods, vanished within a couple of hundred years. A Turkish scientist may have found it again in Greece and Turkey.
Dhaka muslin, woven by sixteen villages from a plant on the banks of the Meghna, had around 1,200 threads to the square inch. A revival has reached 300.
Fogbank, an aerogel inside an American atomic bomb, could not be remade from its own archives, not even by the retired scientists who wrote them.

Artemisinin, now the mainstay of malaria treatment, came from Tu Youyou’s careful reading of an ancient Chinese text. And West Germany and Japan rebuilt after the Second World War with the knowledge their people still carried.
## What survives

Shah’s advice was to watch for records. Recovery depends on “the presence of written records, the presence of samples, the presence of finished Dhaka muslin that you could then aspire to reverse engineer”. {063-C06}
Records alone are not enough. “If you don’t do something for 30, 40 years, then there is a whole range of tacit knowledge that gets lost,” Shah said. {063-C05}
On ancient texts he was blunt. “Two statements are true,” he said. “One, that most of that knowledge is rubbish. Two, that some of it is mind blowingly great.”
Varma drew a rule for tradition: “we should be deeply sceptical of it, but never dismissive.” {063-C09} A remedy earns belief, he said, only once it passes the scientific method.
He also left a riddle. Survivors of the apocalypse find an iPhone 6S thousands of years later, plug it in and read its SMS messages. What will they call them? “Ancient texts.”

second.label: Traditional medicine
second.head: Cold water, hot result
second.deck: Ajay Shah on Tu Youyou, who read an ancient text more carefully
body: In 1974, during the Vietnam War, Tu Youyou was sent to help Vietnam, Ajay Shah said, and its people asked for help with one thing: malaria. {#deputed} The parasite was growing resistant to quinine.

About two thousand plants from ancient Chinese texts had already been tested and failed, and papers said wormwood did not work. Tu was not a PhD, but she was a master of classical Chinese. She read one passage as calling for cold extraction: the plant soaked in water, unheated.

She tried it on twenty patients, and all twenty recovered. {#twenty} Later scientists found the part of the molecule that attacks the parasite and built stronger derivatives. Artemisinin is now the world’s mainstay against malaria. {063-S08}

quote.text: You should remember a woman looking at the misery of malaria in Vietnam and doing research with the wormwood tree in China

second.caption: Tu Youyou’s cold extraction

third.head: Guard duty, reason unknown
body: An army camp keeps a guard beside a garden bench 24 hours a day, changing shifts every eight hours. The bench has no strategic or tactical significance. Amit Varma told the story after the Fogbank tale.
A new commandant asks why. The guard has been told to stand there. The deputy has no idea. Previous commandants say it has always been like this.
Obsessed, the commandant tracks down the camp’s founder, now 93 and bedridden on a farm, flies out in economy and talks his way past the worried wife. {#ninetythree}
Why, he asks, does a guard stand beside the bench? The old man looks at him with wizened eyes. “What are you saying? The paint hasn’t dried yet.” {063-S07}
third.caption: the guard and the bench

p2.title: Lost and found
p2.deck: Five quests for vanished knowledge, and the lessons Amit Varma and Ajay Shah drew from them

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: Naked, clever and helpless
sections.caption: the wicked witch’s challenge
body: Amit Varma brought the question from a WhatsApp group: a post by the writer Tim Urban about a wicked witch who makes every material good on Earth vanish, and promises it all back once humanity builds one working iPhone 6S. {063-R01}

Urban, Varma said, built up to it on Lex Fridman’s podcast by noting that no human being knows how to make a pencil. Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil* tells the story from the pencil’s side: so many countries, materials and kinds of knowledge go into it that no one person can make one. {063-R03}

“Self-sufficiency is a myth,” Varma said. What we have instead is a “magnificent complicated interlinked web of knowledge and people and specialisation”. {063-C02} Frédéric Bastiat, he noted, wrote about how Paris gets fed with no one planning it.
## Prices as technology

Rebuilding would need more than machines, Varma argued. It would need what he called social technology: prices, for instance, which carry information and incentives between people who never meet, as Friedrich Hayek explained in *The Use of Knowledge in Society*. {063-C03}

Ajay Shah thought the witch’s challenge could never be met. Without markets and institutions, people would turn on each other, as in Cormac McCarthy’s *The Road*, and the world population would crash to 10 million. {#tenmillion}
~ A new scientific civilisation would arise, Shah said, but it would not retrace the precise journey to semiconductors, integrated circuits and touch screens.

quote.text: There is no way to feed seven and a half billion people without the glories of the market economy and modern civilisation

sections.label: Quest one
sections.head: Food of the gods, gone
sections.caption: the lost Roman herb
body: The Romans wrote and wrote and wrote, Ajay Shah said, recipes included. Their texts prize a herb called silphium, which grew in what they called Carthage and we call Libya. Nobody could cultivate it, so foragers gathered it from the wild, and it fetched the highest prices.
Within a couple of hundred years it was gone; legend has it that the last plant went to the Emperor Nero. {063-S04} Amit Varma added that Pliny the Elder recorded this in his *Natural History*.
## A modern second chance

Expeditions into Libya’s remotest mountains found nothing. Then a Turkish scientist found a plant of the Ferula family in remote parts of Greece and Turkey that looks a lot like the ancient drawings. Food connoisseurs fed the old recipes call the results mind-blowing.

Without ancient biological material there can be no DNA test, Shah said. But modern science has done what the Romans could not: “they have applied tools of modern science to figure out how to cultivate this in a greenhouse.” {#greenhouse}
~ The find is being kept quiet for now, Shah said, lest a stampede of foragers, and specimens on eBay, drive the plant extinct a second time. {#ebay}

quote.text: It would be lovely to not lose our knowledge.

sections.label: Quest two
sections.head: Many hands, no notebook
sections.caption: how a cloth was forgotten
body: Amit Varma, a Bengali, took up a Bengali loss. Dhaka muslin came from a plant on the banks of the Meghna and took sixteen villages to make, each doing one part of the work. {#sixteen}

Each village knew its own stage, and nobody wrote the process down. When the trade died, the knowledge was lost within a generation. {063-S05} “There is no Pliny the Elder to write down all the processes,” Varma said.
## Clues in a museum

Recovery, Ajay Shah said, depends on what survives. Here it was plant samples in a London herbarium, which could be sequenced, and finished cloth in the Victoria and Albert Museum. “It’s just that we don’t know how to make them,” he said. {063-C06}

With such clues and modern genetics, a revival has managed 300 threads to the square inch. {#threehundred} Varma called its air-conditioned weaving hut a modern jugaad: the sixteen villages had nothing of the kind.
~ But “three hundred to twelve hundred is a long way”, Varma said. Anyone buying the new cloth must decide whether to compromise on the threads, or wait for the science to get there.

quote.text: That knowledge is lost in a generation and they go on to do other things and the knowledge is completely lost.

sections.label: Quest three
sections.head: Use it or lose it
sections.caption: why know-how needs practice
body: Fogbank, Ajay Shah said, was lost under very optimistic conditions: military levels of bureaucracy and record-keeping, and the original scientists still around. Stop doing something for 30 or 40 years, and the tacit knowledge goes anyway. {063-C05}
Nuclear bombs, he explained, do not keep the way a bullet or an artillery shell does. They contain electrical parts and batteries, and need a complex maintenance schedule.
## A Russian hypothesis

That led Shah to a hypothesis some people genuinely hold. The knowledge of that maintenance may have evaporated when the Soviet Union collapsed, and “it is possible that there is not a single working nuclear bomb in Russia today”. {#russia}
He called it a reasonable hypothesis. The lesson, he said, is to store and log such knowledge; but if nobody is actively doing something, it will go away.
Amit Varma was reminded of an army camp where a guard stood beside a bench for decades because nobody remembered the reason. {#reminded}

~ Shah wondered whether the episode was made of stories that ought to be movies. “These could all be movies, actually,” Varma said. “There’s so much human drama surrounding each of these,” Shah replied.

quote.text: This kind of knowledge is precious and we should do all we can to store it and log it.

sections.label: Quest four
sections.head: Mostly rubbish, sometimes gold
sections.caption: ancient texts and modern tests
body: Ancient texts, Ajay Shah said, are “cool and funny. They’re intended as humour.” They hold the occasional nugget of amazing truth, and only testing finds it: some two thousand plants from traditional Chinese texts failed against malaria before one worked. {#twothousand}
Yet Shah warned against the opposite error. “I think in the modern world we are a little too arrogant in that we think we fabricate everything,” he said. {063-C08}

Citing James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, Shah said about half of the world’s 20 most important drugs, including quinine, artemisinin and metformin, began with plants and the knowledge of traditional people. {063-R14}
Modern science deserves credit for refining them, he added. Turning a flower into a precise 500 mg slow-release pill is a great feat. {#metformin}
## Survivor bias

Amit Varma would treat tradition with deep scepticism, but never dismiss it. {063-C09} Focusing only on the successes is survivor bias, he said: “the two thousand plants that did not pass the test are also important.”
~ Old knowledge systems, Varma added, built theories on first principles that came from a complete lack of what science knows today, so extending them gets you nowhere.

quote.text: Respect tradition but always be sceptical.

sections.label: Quest five
sections.head: Flattened, then flourishing
sections.caption: Germany and Japan after the war
body: By 1945 Germany and Japan lay in ruins, Ajay Shah said: factories destroyed, Tokyo’s wooden houses firebombed, and Germany’s institutions first taken over by the Nazis, then wrecked in the war. It was, he said, “a bit of an iPhone and Wicked Witch casting a spell idea”.
The knowledge in people’s heads was considerable. In 1933, Shah noted, Germany had more Nobel laureates than the UK. {#nobel}
## Records and rights
West Germany had help that Urban’s naked humans lack. Under the Marshall Plan money was available, and books and manuals could be printed abroad and brought back. {#marshall}

Records were kept, so pre-war shareholders were honoured. “So imagine there is a second world war, there’s complete devastation, every factory is gone, and Volkswagen comes back,” Shah said. {063-S11}

An old Weimar draft, with pacifism added, became the new constitution. Japan, after a successful period of American rule, got a pacifist constitution too. East Germany, under communist rule, never quite recovered.

Amit Varma gave much of the credit to Ludwig Erhard, Adenauer’s finance minister, who understood the value of freedom and property rights. In that Germany, Varma said, “all the things we would dream of for India actually happened.” {063-S12}
~ Both countries, Shah said, decisively turned their backs on nationalism and militarism, and reinvented themselves.

quote.text: I would not have been able to predict how well West Germany was going to take off

side.boxText: Tim Urban’s iPhone thought experiment reached Amit Varma when a friend shared it in a four-man WhatsApp group called Food Lovers of Mumbai. It shows how much of what we know depends on a web no one could quickly rebuild. {063-R01}

contQuote.text: All your material goods are gone, but your knowledge is still in your head. And you can get everything back. All you need to do is build an iPhone six.

p3.title: Tales of the lost
p3.deck: Four stories of knowledge vanishing, and of the people hunting it down

stories.start: And she starts off by talking about a scandal in 18th century Britain.
stories.end: revive this tradition, but three hundred to twelve hundred is a long way
stories.caption: Dhaka muslin’s lost threads
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a scandalous fabric and its slow return
stories.head: Sixteen villages, one lost cloth
body: At the end of the 18th century, Amit Varma said, reading from the *Encyclopedia Americana*, women’s dress swapped stiff damasks, velvets, satins and silks for the clinging, short-waisted muslin gown. It caused a scandal in Britain.

A satire from around 1801 has a lady ask a milliner how to be dressed in the latest fashion. He has her remove her bonnet, her tunic, her petticoat and her corset, and announces: “In these days, if you want to be well dressed, you have to be well undressed.” {063-J05}
The finest of the fabric was Dhaka muslin, from a plant on the banks of the Meghna in Bengal. Ordinary muslin has 20 to 40 threads per square inch. {#threads} Dhaka muslin had around 1,200.
Sixteen villages made it, each doing one stage of the work. When the trade died, the know-how vanished within a generation, and the plant itself could no longer be found. {063-S05}

The revival began with a 19th-century leaf. Researchers analysed its DNA, scanned the Meghna’s banks with satellite imagery, and found a plant that shared 70 per cent of the original’s DNA. {#seventy}

Then they went to weavers across Bangladesh. Told the thread count, the weavers balked. One agreed. Housed in a temperature-controlled hut, he produced a version with 300 threads. {#threehundred} Dresses made from it have sold for thousands of dollars.
~ Varma left Ajay Shah with a shopping dilemma for his next dress for Susan: compromise on the threads and still spend lots of money, or wait for the science to get there.
stories.why: Knowledge spread across many specialised hands, with nobody writing the process down, can vanish within a generation. Getting it back takes surviving samples, finished cloth to reverse-engineer and modern science, and even then the recovery is partial. {063-C06}
stories.postscript: A friend of the hosts, Varma said, came up with “the big bong theory”: that everything really started with big bongs. {063-J04}

stories.caption: the Fogbank fiasco
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the atomic recipe America could not follow
stories.head: The bomb that forgot its recipe
body: Aerogels are the lightest materials known, Ajay Shah said: a litre might weigh two or three grams. {#aerogel} For one kind of American atomic bomb, built 40 or 50 years ago, a special aerogel was developed under the code name Fogbank.

During a maintenance overhaul some five or ten years ago, the United States found it had run out of Fogbank. Scientists went to the archives, project reports and experiment logs, and could not make it.

So retired scientists were brought in and handed their own documents. “You bloody now deliver, you make Fogbank using your documents,” Shah said. “These old hippies, they tried their magic, but no Fogbank.” {063-J10}
~ With auditors screaming, about $70 million went into a brand new research project to reach the same aerogel from scratch. {#seventymillion}
stories.why: Even with military levels of bureaucracy and record-keeping, and with the original scientists still alive, know-how that had stopped being practised for 30 or 40 years could not be recovered from documents alone. {063-S06}

stories.start: In the h history of Rome, they wrote and saved a lot of documents.
stories.end: So I though I am waiting with bated breath
stories.caption: silphium and hing
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a Roman luxury and an Indian staple
stories.head: Hing, the poor man’s silphium
body: Silphium was the Romans’ prized herb, Ajay Shah said. They used its flowers, its stalk and its resinous gum, and could only forage it from the wild. Within a couple of hundred years, it was gone. {063-S04}
The Roman texts also name a backup for anyone too cheap or too poor to buy silphium resin: a cheap, harsh, pungent substitute. “That backup plan was hing,” Shah said. {#hing}
Hing, or asafoetida, is a Ferula, and so is the plant a Turkish scientist has found in Greece and Turkey. “So this also connects,” Shah said.

~ Hing, he said, is “an absolute paradise in Indian cooking”. If silphium returns, he imagines Roman recipes meeting Indian ones: perhaps a better curd rice made with ferula resin. He is waiting “with bated breath”.

quote.text: You feel the loss, you feel the hurt that there was something beautiful that we knew and it was lost.

stories.start: So the discovery of coffee. is because some shepherd in Ethioptic
stories.end: aborigines are able to observe the animals and get this kind of knowledge
stories.caption: goats, gorillas and coffee
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on knowledge borrowed from goats and gorillas
stories.head: Follow the frisky goats
body: The story of coffee begins in Ethiopia, Ajay Shah said, with a shepherd who noticed that his goats turned unusually frisky after eating the plant’s berries. They would jump around and have a good time. {#goats}
So he tried chewing them himself, and through hundreds of years of random experiments people got to roasting.
Scientists, Shah added, have seen something similar in the wild. “A gorilla gets a stomach upset. The gorilla walks 15 kilometres, finds one particular plant, and eats it.” {063-S09}

~ Indigenous peoples, Shah said, gain exactly this kind of knowledge by watching animals. The knowledge of the forest is now “rapidly vanishing”, and “we should do all we can to protect that knowledge”.
stories.why: Much human knowledge was gathered by watching nature rather than invented in laboratories. Coffee and medicines alike began this way, and the forest peoples who hold such knowledge are losing it fast.

quiz.q: What must humanity build, in Tim Urban’s thought experiment, to undo the wicked witch’s spell?
quiz.a: One working iPhone 6S, with all their knowledge but no material goods.

quiz.q: How many threads per square inch did the original Dhaka muslin have, against ordinary muslin’s twenty to forty?

quiz.q: What did retired American scientists fail to make, even when handed their own documents?

quiz.q: How did Tu Youyou read the ancient Chinese text on wormwood differently from others?
